articles.description: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. articles.title: Scorned Trump boots Rwanda, South Africa from trade deal
articles.description: Last week, the Trump administration announced that, beginning January 1, South Africa and Rwanda will stop receiving preferential trade access to the U.S. market through the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). Rather, in both cases, their removal from AGOA serves as an act of retribution from a president unhappy with their governments’ policies on domestic or regional issues. But American interests themselves will suffer, as consumers will be forced to pay higher prices for the same goods. articles.title: Three Men & A Photo Op: What To Expect In Shenzhen
articles.description: Three Men & A Photo Op: What To Expect In Shenzhen Authored by Larry C. Johnson via Sonar21 , On Thursday, November 19, in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, Donald Trump will sit down with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping for a three-way conversation . Beijing's Foreign Ministry made it official on Monday, calling it the "China-Russia-United States Summit." The Kremlin had already announced it, and the White House had already bragged about it. It really is a first. No American president has ever sat at the same table with the leaders in Moscow and Beijing. Not FDR, who saw Stalin at Tehran and Yalta and saw China's Chiang Kai-shek separately in Cairo. Not Nixon, who went to Beijing and Moscow on separate trips in 1972. Not Reagan or the Bushes. All three of today's leaders sat through the same G20 group photos in Trump's first term, but never at the same negotiating table. Washington's foreign policy establishment is already muttering about a "new Yalta." So what will actually happen? You don't need a crystal ball. You need a calendar. Trump has now held four in-person summits with these two men since August 2025, and they follow a script so predictable you could set your watch by it.

Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) confirmed of the early Tuesday event (local time), that several Russian planes were observed briefly entering the country's air defense identification zone (ADIZ) . Prior file image While it wasn't a breach of national airspace per se, commanders in Seoul identified the inbound aircraft as a potential threat. "The South Korean military detected the Russian aircraft before they entered the KADIZ and deployed fighter jets to prepare for any possible contingencies , the JCS said in a statement," according to Yonhap News Agency. The Russian planes later exited the zone but did not violate South Korean airspace, the statement noted. No notice was given by the inbound aircraft. articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
articles.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. They were knee-length, give or take an inch up or down, and A-line, although sometimes a narrow almost-pencil and other times with a broader flare. There were skirts that wrapped like kilts, held together with strips of industrial-weight Velcro embroidered with tiny gems. articles.title: Dream of Birds – documentary
articles.description: What happens when a forest loses its birdsong? Following clues hidden in the sounds birds make while asleep , Argentinian physicist Gabriel Mindlin uncovers a hidden extinction – not of species, but of memory – and sets out to revive vanished melodies before they disappear forever. Part detective story, part cutting-edge science, Mindlin’s mission leads him to the dusty 1960s archives of Buenos Aires naturalist, confirming that some songs no longer echo in the biosphere. So he deploys “robot tutors” to see whether young birds can learn and spread the old songs once again. Read more on this topic: Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs? Continue reading...

articles.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
articles.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
articles.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘All I could smell was fertiliser’: the best (and worst) supermarket instant coffee, tasted and rated
articles.description: Our coffee snob spills the beans on which granules hint at chocolate and caramel, and which leave a bitter note • Everything you need to make great coffee I’m a coffee snob with my own grinder, but I found the haptic thwack, whack and crack of opening the lid and film on a jar of instant coffee strangely invigorating, and rather nostalgic. When I took a deep sniff, however, disaster: all I could smell was fertiliser! Instant coffee is brewed at scorching temperatures, then either freeze-dried in a vacuum or spray-dried using hot air. This industrial process strips away many of the volatile flavour compounds and bright aromas that make fresh coffee smell so good. This gives it an earthier, muskier and more bitter flavour profile, though, thankfully, with a little alchemy and hot water, those more familiar coffee aromas and flavours returned, with notes of chicory, bitter chocolate and burnt sugar. Almost all of these products have a similar industrial imprint, uniform granules and a one-dimensional flavour profile, so they’re ultimately more a simulation of the real thing. That said, some did surprise me. At best, they taste like a cup of office filter coffee, made in a commercial d

articles.title: ‘You have to cope’: why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
articles.description: The world has become accustomed to concerns about the male loneliness epidemic. But research suggests women are just as lonely Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads No one would think of Sasha* as lonely, least of all Sasha herself. The 38-year-old from Sydney has close and longstanding friendships, proactively keeps in touch and makes plans, and is engaged with her local community. “All those things that you read about, about why men might be lonely – they don’t maintain one-on-one friendships, or they’re not good at reaching out, or their conversations aren’t deep and meaningful – none of those issues apply to me,” she says. “I’m a very socially connected person.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Like many men of his generation, he tends to push his feelings down from his heart to his toes’: Meera Sodha on her father’s homecoming
articles.description: After a childhood of grief, hardship and hunger, the Guardian food writer’s father Raj always resisted going back to Uganda. What happened when he finally agreed to accompany her on a bittersweet journey into the past? The moment I step off the plane and on to the soil of Entebbe it hits me. Uganda is in my blood. This country that had once existed only in my imagination is finally real. The heat is heavy, the earth bright and rich like dark terracotta. I want to capture this moment – me with my 75-year-old dad, back where he was born. A place he never imagined he would return to. I whoop and reach for my camera, turn it towards my father’s face. “You’re back!” I say. Continue reading...

articles.title: Blacklock, Birmingham B3: ‘A very, very cool version of an Angus Steakhouse’ – restaurant review
articles.description: Ever-open, eminently relatable, sensibly priced spots of this sort will always have an audience A London chophouse has taken up residence on St Philip’s Place, Birmingham, on the edge of Cathedral Square, or “Pigeon Park”, as the locals call it. This particular nook of Brum city centre is a magnet to those feathered blighters, although Blacklock ’s smoulderingly macho menu is ironically pigeon-meat free, revolving instead around heaps of chops and steaks cooked over charcoal. There’s porterhouse, bone-in sirloin, lamb rump and pig’s head on toast. Launched in London in 2015 , Blacklock was the elegant, edgy, no-nonsense dining experience for groovy young things who quite literally wanted meat and two veg, so long as said veg was dripping-fat chips; it now has five sites in the capital and another in Manchester. “We just ended up at Blacklock,” people used to tell me half a dozen times a week, then go on to rave about the bread, the gravy and the ash-baked sweet potatoes, and revel in the glorious simplicity of it all. Modern life was complex, Blacklock was not, but neither was it cheap enough to feel like a jaunt down the Toby Carvery . And now its big flavours and broad appeal hav

articles.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. T

articles.title: ‘I was nervous before my solo stay in a remote Scottish Highlands cabin – but the solitude is glorious’
articles.description: As a lone female traveller, the prospect of staying in a hut on Rannoch Moor is daunting, but the silence of the mountains and lochs turns out to be ‘the ultimate luxury’ In the gloaming, the trees stand dark and impenetrable on either side of the path. An owl, wide-faced and pale as a spectre, glides out of the pines ahead of me. Heart pounding, I pick up speed and continue uphill, the silence thick around me. Just a few minutes earlier, I had been scuffing my feet in the sand by the loch shore, watching as the clouds draped themselves across the top of the Grampians. In the absence of other people, Loch Laidon, silvery in the half-light, had been mine to enjoy; in the woods, however, my solitude feels unnerving. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: The 14 best men’s boots for winter, from chelseas and lace-ups to wellies

For years I wrote them off – at 5ft 8in, I was convinced anything above the ankle would make my legs look shorter. Then I started wearing them with the right trousers – a straight leg that falls over the top – and realised I’d spent a decade getting winter wrong. All anyone sees is a smart pair of shoes that happens to keep your ankles warm. Here’s the thing: boots needn’t be intimidating. They’re just the wintry version of the leather shoes you already own. A chelsea is your loafer – it goes with pretty much everything in your wardrobe and every event in your diary, Christmas parties included. A derby boot is laced up, a bit sturdier and just as happy with jeans. The chukka is your weekend trainer. And the chunky, rubber-soled ones? Just think of them as an umbrella for your feet. articles.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?

The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. articles.title: ‘I’m a smalltown girl with a terrible disability. He’s a Hollywood superstar. But we’ve been laughing since we met’: Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell on their extraordinary story
articles.description: She has a rare debilitating skin condition but still tackled a marathon, helped by her old friend. As new film The Slightest Touch tells the full story of that emotional day, its stars talk about their lifelong bond – and why he opened up about parenthood Last month, HBO sent a private jet to Dublin to fly the star of a new documentary to London for the premiere. Colin Farrell appears in the film. But the private jet was not for him. The VIP passenger was Emma Fogarty, who has a rare, incurable genetic skin condition, epidermolysis bullosa or EB. Taking a commercial flight would have been physically impossible for her. As a publicist working on the film whispered to me, it was the one time you can emit all that carbon with a clean conscience. Fogarty was born 42 years ago. When she was diagnosed with EB, her parents were told she was unlikely to survive a week – which was probably for the best, said the doctor. With EB, the proteins that hold the layers of skin together are missing or faulty, leaving it as fragile as a butterfly’s wings. The slightest knock or bang can cause the skin to tear or blister; 80% of Fogarty’s body is without skin, and is wrapped in bandages to protect th

articles.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
articles.description: Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats. As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world , this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009. Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
articles.description: She threw a (metaphorical) brick through Spotify’s window and exposed industry failings with her ‘Butts for Tour Buses’ campaign. Now the singer is embracing her Irish roots with her new album’s fighting spirit Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour. That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.” [see footnote] Continue reading...

articles.description: In this week’s newsletter: what the death of Cheikh Hamidou Kane reveals about the cultural gap, plus Iran’s rising use of executions to curb dissent After reading about the death of the Senegalese writer Cheikh Hamidou Kane this week, I went on a mission to find his most famous book. Described as a master of the pan-African novel and a literary giant, the 98-year-old received obituaries internationally, and in both French- and English-language African media. Le Monde called him “iconic”. His 1961 book L’Aventure Ambiguë (Ambiguous Adventure) has been studied in numerous universities and schools across the continent and is said to be one of the best books by an African writer to capture the post-colonial struggle for identity in newly independent countries. articles.title: Gianni Schicchi review – fraud, fun and farce with the gutsy Mid Wales Opera
articles.description: Theatr Brycheiniog, Brecon Puccini’s short comic opera comes to life with Richard Studer’s touring production, which leans into its commedia dell-arte elements In Dante’s Inferno, Gianni Schicchi de’ Cavalcanti, a 13th-century Florentine knight, was consigned to the eighth circle of hell for having been an arch-impostor. Puccini’s Gianni Schicchi, however, gets away with his blatant fraud, impersonating the newly deceased Buoso Donati and cheating his greedy relatives out of a large part of their rich uncle’s inheritance – albeit that they plotted with him to overturn the original will – to bag the best for himself. In this last of the Il Trittico triptych, Puccini allowed himself a lot of fun, and that too was the main ingredient in Mid Wales Opera’s SmallStages touring production. Tightly choreographed, with comedic energy and over-the-top characterisations, the commedia dell’arte element here bordered on farce, not least as the lugubrious crocodile tears of the shameless relatives waving their Pavarotti handkerchiefs gave way to boisterous remonstrations on learning that the whole estate had been left to a monastery. Continue reading...

articles.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
articles.description: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples. Cont

articles.title: Squash and chickpea curry, and whipped beans with radicchio: Marie Mitchell’s sweet-and-sour recipes
articles.description: Pucker up for squash and tamarind curry with stewed chickpeas and coriander, or how about whipped cannellini beans with leeks, roast radicchio and parmesan? Who doesn’t love sweet and sour? If you’re complaining that you don’t right now, then you’re lying – it’s an almost perfect pairing. Here, I’m playing with the sweet-and-sour notes of vinegar and the tang of tamarind in two dishes that are on repeat in our house. Dinners for when you want to spend more time on the sofa and less time in the kitchen. Continue reading...

I am entitled to shared accommodation allowance as I am under 35 and claim universal credit. However, the DWP is paying me the higher one-bedroom rate for couples. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tell us: have you been misdiagnosed with a medical condition?
articles.description: We are looking for people to share their stories of misdiagnosis, how they realised this had happened, and perhaps found another diagnosis Last month the actor Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis . She announced that she had the condition in 2021, and has spoken candidly about her experiences of it, becoming a prominent advocate for people living with MS. “I’m back at square one ... I don’t know what’s going on with me.” Applegate said on her podcast MeSsy, adding: “There’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old. There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service , careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation , scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold , the leisure centres closed , the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back . That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. Let that begin here. Polly

articles.title: Miliband plays warm-up man for Burnham’s big Brexit speech | John Crace
articles.description: The foreign secretary played his cards carefully as the PM prepared to tell us he wants a reset with Europe So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past. Brexit is the wound that will never heal, despite the ministrations of countless Grail knights. More than 10 years have passed and still our politics is defined by the sliding doors moment of the EU referendum. Everything dragging us back to that June day in 2016. The further we get from it, the closer it becomes. Something only Stephen Hawking could have explained. And then, only to himself. The rest of us would have been none the wiser. For the most part, we’ve tried to avoid talking about the subject. At least in public. It’s considered impolite, an intrusion into a national grief. In private, most people now admit the country is worse off than we were before we left the EU. But it is a pain and misfortune that must be borne stoically. The people had spoken. And the people can never be wrong. Except when they are. The Guardian’s year in review 2026 . On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Guardian’s

articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
articles.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting

articles.title: Though Trump is giving him the cold shoulder, Netanyahu is pulling out all the stops to cling to power. And he just might | Simon Tisdall
articles.description: The downfall of the Israeli PM may seem inevitable now; it is anything but. He must be ejected from office and brought to justice It’s unsporting to kick a man when he’s down. But let’s make an exception for Benjamin Netanyahu. Ever since his far-right coalition government lost its mandate in last month’s national elections, Israel’s prime minister has been making an ugly spectacle of himself. His antics resemble those of a condemned man, desperately scrabbling to escape the gallows. This might not matter so much if, as has been widely assumed (and hoped), Netanyahu cannot ultimately avoid the drop. Yet h is final downfall remains far from certain. As protracted, complex talks proceed over who will form Israel’s next administration – certain to be some variety of multiparty coalition – Netanyahu, forced for now into a nominal caretaker role, is going to extraordinary lengths to cling to power, using every dirty trick in his well-thumbed handbook while calling for a “government of national unity” (excluding Arab parties). And the perception he has been hung out to dry by a similarly electorally humbled Donald Trump , his biggest ally, may also prove over-optimistic. Besieged Palesti

articles.title: Police ‘retreating from streets’ due to major funding crisis, chief constables say
articles.description: Forces across England and Wales struggle amid financial pressures described as worst for decades Police chiefs say officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst financial crisis in decades, which has left nine forces seeking exceptional financial support (EFS) from the government. Paul Sanford, the chief constable of Norfolk police and the finance lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), said exceptional financial support was needed if forces across England and Wales were to remain operationally viable. articles.description: PM’s spokesperson calls message, read out by convicted rapist’s wife on their YouTube channel, ‘clearly appalling’ The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction . Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her rapist husband in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Woman accusing David Walliams of grooming her backs staggered age of consent call
articles.description: Comments come after Mia Latter, who alleged she was raped by Russell Brand, had said she wanted a change in law A woman who has accused David Walliams of grooming her has said she supports a staggered age of consent. Walliams, 55, has been accused of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex, a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found. Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . The National Association for People Abused in Childhood ( Napac ) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse , childhood abuse , and people in crisis . The ITV News documentary David Walliams: Power and Silence is available to watch on YouTube and ITVX. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 draft text is attempt to ‘draw out parties’ to find agreement, president of talks says
articles.description: Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said. Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”. Continue reading...

articles.title: AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports
articles.description: While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged Cop31 live – latest updates Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study. While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO 2 is not the main driver of climate change”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Naming your feelings can be harder than you think. This simple tool can help
articles.description: About 10% of people have significant trouble identifying their emotions – which makes it harder to know what to do about them Naming emotions is a core skill that most people develop as children, and it might seem like second nature. But research indicates that it’s harder than you think – about 10% of the general population have significant difficulty identifying their own emotions. That’s why a simple tool called the feelings wheel has gained popularity in therapists’ offices and classrooms over recent years. Continue reading...

articles.title: Russell Brand: Open Secret review – ​a real tribute to the journalists and victims who brought him to justice
articles.description: This Netflix documentary offers a fascinating look at how Brand’s behaviour wasn’t simply tolerated; it was actively celebrated Last week was quite the week. Coming within a few days of each other, the sentencing of Russell Brand and the allegations about David Walliams have felt dizzying. As well as all the elation that justice has been served in relation to Brand, and the admiration for the women who saw that it was, there’s also an underlying sense of exhaustion about the sheer grubbiness of it all. With this in mind, the thought of watching a feature-length documentary about the Sunday Times and Channel 4’s investigation into Brand might feel like willingly dunking your head into a toilet. However, Russell Brand: Open Secret is absolutely worth an hour and a half of your time. Not only is the film a tribute to Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, the journalists who spent years meticulously drawing the net closer to Brand – and, needless to say, to his victims – but it does a tremendous job of putting the whole sorry affair into a broader cultural context. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘These men feel protected’: how Mexico’s first femicide squad is turning the tide on record killings
articles.description: The female-led unit in Mexico City has cut gender-based murders from a historic high in 2021. Now, there are hopes to appoint specialist teams and prosecutors nationwide Paz Rodríguez woke up about 5am at her home in Milpa Alta, a suburb of Mexico City, on 20 March 2021. She thought about her plans for the day: pick up yellow lilies and cacti from her mother’s house and sell them in the market. Later that evening, they would cook mole , a traditional Mexican dish, together. She reached for her phone, which was flooded with texts from her sister, Oliviera Rodríguez. “Mum’s dog is barking a lot,” she had written. “I keep calling and she won’t respond.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘George Michael came out of his coma talking like Jill’: Julia Davis and Rebecca Front on their squirm-inducing comedy Nighty Night
articles.description: ‘When Jill and Glen are in bed, that was Steve Coogan’s bed. He was rarely there so we didn’t bother washing the sheets afterwards’ It all started with the character of Jill Tyrell. I’d done Human Remains [a black comedy about oddball couples] with Rob Brydon and was trying to write something of my own. I remembered this woman from Human Remains called Beverley. She was in her 50s, from the West Country and did home hairdressing. She told a client: “The ammonia will burn your ears a bit, Joyce, that’s completely natural.” Bath and Bristol are embedded in my history, so I thought I’d develop that. I made Jill two decades younger and gave her husband Terry cancer, which she uses to her advantage. Continue reading...

articles.description: Every year I receive a letter from the daughter of a patient I treated. It’s an act of unbelievable grace in a job that often feels thankless Many years ago, in early November, I received a note. It read: “Dear Doctor, Dad would have been 78 years old today. Of course, no amount of time would have been enough. We think of him and miss him every day.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
articles.description: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
articles.description: Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “ welcome back ” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “ Breturn ” has yet to catch on. By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to

articles.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
articles.description: From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “ war minus the shooting ”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday? Even those who don’t understand the finer points of the rolling maul can surely grasp why this result matters. For much of the last century, heavy industry and rugby were twin pillars of Welsh national identity. The heavy industry is largely gone, and over the past few years, rugby has looked to be going the same way: a weakened national team; financial problems that threatened to tear apart th

articles.title: Damaging the lifeline that Samaritans offers the public | Letters
articles.description: Volunteers despair as the charity sets about closing local branches and restructuring Samaritans old and new will, I’m sure, have been just as shocked as I was by your article ( ‘Is anyone up for a fight?’: The battle for the soul of Samaritans, 10 November ). Many, though, will not be surprised. I was a volunteer for 26 years in three branches. The work was demanding and life-changing; the experience is so transformative that it gives every part of society people who are strong enough to bear others’ burdens and able to share their pain. We don’t stop being listeners when we stop being volunteers. During my time, I found that the people at the top were detached from what went on at branch level. It is not news to me that they cannot understand how central to the work each local branch is and how important every human contact is to those who need to talk. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why Alan Milburn’s Pip plan is a mistake | Letters
articles.description: Savitri Hensman says financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest Alan Milburn has a track record of so-called cost-cutting measures that waste billions of pounds in public money while making health worse. The private finance initiative was an expensive mess , though it did help huge companies and rich people get richer. It is less surprising that he wants more benefits for young sick and disabled people slashed than that the government might go along with this ( Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund, 12 November ). Financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest. The high number of young people not in education, employment or training is probably largely due to past top-level decisions. Austerity, making life tougher for claimants while favouring multimillionaires, fewer youth clubs, underfunded mental health care, long delays in providing assessments and equipment, and making school and university more stressful have not only caused suffering but also been expensive. Continue reading...

articles.title: A fair deal on fees for EU and UK students | Letters
articles.description: Thomas Altebaeumer notes that under the proposed scheme, UK students in Europe would pay domestic fees, as EU students studying in the UK would Vicky Wolmuth is angered that the UK government is able to find £450m to subsidise UK universities for admitting EU students while UK students are struggling with student debt ( Letters, 10 November ). She appears to have missed that, under the proposed scheme, UK students in Europe would pay domestic fees, just as EU students studying in the UK would. Fees in the UK are among the highest in Europe. This is a political choice. Continue reading...

articles.title: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest | Letters
articles.description: Joanna Elson of the Independent Age charity is concerned about poverty among pensioners and says ministers need to think hard before making changes You report ( 11 November ) Torsten Bell’s suggestion that the Conservatives would need to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock. It is well known that raising the state pension age increases poverty rates among those who have to wait longer for it, with those on the lowest incomes hit the hardest. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported that when the age rose from 65 to 66, the poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled, with renters and those with lower levels of education among those more likely to struggle. Continue reading...

articles.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
articles.description: Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14. So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life. Continue reading...

articles.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
articles.description: Grand Palais, Paris The fair celebrated the bicentenary of photography – but did anyone care? Especially when the most compelling images proposed whole new ways of seeing No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist. This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance. Continue reading...

articles.title: Souped-up and now on screen, Starlight Express is moving in all sorts of ways
articles.description: Luke Sheppard’s revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 80s musical is in cinemas and going on tour. What gives these ridiculous, rollerskating trains such emotional force? I hardly ever cry at the theatre but can think of three recent cases. 1. The beautifully jittery balcony scene in Liverpool Everyman’s Romeo and Juliet . 2. Dear Theodosia as co-sung by Leslie Odom Jr (actual OG Aaron Burr!) in Hamilton . 3. An embarrassingly large amount of Starlight Express . Why on earth does this ridiculous fantasy of rollerskating trains, with their high-speed scrapes, leave me feeling like an emotional wreck? That’s what happened when I first saw director Luke Sheppard’s souped-up London revival – and again this month, watching a new film of that production. Continue reading...

articles.title: Eurovision organisers criticise Malaysian removal of LGBT+ footage in first Asian contest
articles.description: Broadcaster TV3 appears to cut footage of Thai drag performers and gay Philippine jury spokesperson Eurovision’s organisers have said they are “surprised and disappointed” that the first Eurovision Asia was altered when it was broadcast in Malaysia, apparently removing LGBTQ+ imagery and people from the show. The European Broadcasting Union (EBU), the alliance of public broadcasters that owns Eurovision, said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the Asian contest under licence, and ask it to establish with the Malaysian broadcaster TV3 why it happened. Continue reading...

articles.title: From pyjama parades to blind biscuit taste tests: how we made our ultimate festive gift guide
articles.description: We spent months putting hundreds of presents to the test – here is how we whittled them down • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 If you struggle with the idea of Christmas creep – when the festive season appears to start earlier every year – spare a thought for the team here at Filter HQ. We’ve been in Christmas mode since we packed away last year’s decorations, testing hundreds of presents for our magnum opus: the big 2026 Christmas gift guide . All 369 (we did say it was big) gifts on this year’s list were put through their paces by a crack team of testers covering all ages and tastes. Fashion writer and stylist Sam Deaman – who tested men’s accessories and nightwear – says his partner got fed up with him parading “yet another” pair of pyjamas around their bedroom each night: “It was like Stars in Their Eyes for Christmas gifts,” he says. “‘Tonight, Matthew, I’m going to be … Ebenezer Scrooge!’” Continue reading...

articles.title: Jess Elliott Dennison’s quick and easy recipe for ricotta dumplings with sage butter, rocket and lemon | Quick and easy
articles.description: Easy cheesy dumplings with the perfect level of lightness and squidge Making gnocchi from scratch can be a bit of a faff midweek. However, these ricotta-and-parmesan-based dumplings are so easy to throw together, and always come out light and with just the right amount of squidge. Sage and brown butter feels the right sauce at this time of year, but you could serve them with a simple tomato sauce instead. Any leftover dumplings work a treat thrown into a brothy, minestrone-type soup. Continue reading...

articles.title: The one change that worked: I was burnt out and lonely – until I started ice skating
articles.description: I was stressed and newly diagnosed with ADHD when I decided to choose a new hobby. It awakened my playfulness and immediately improved my quality of life In 2024, I decided to return to England after four and a half years in Lisbon. My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living. During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. I felt overwhelmed and would shut down, which would lead to cycles of anxiety, depression and self-criticism. Continue reading...

articles.title: I Am Helen review – Nicola Coughlan is absolutely superb in this terrifying must-watch
articles.description: After the week we’ve had, you may not feel ready to watch this brilliantly powerful film about the toxic manosphere and its impact on relationships. But do make the time I would understand, after the week in the news we’ve had, if you were not feeling quite ready to deal with the new instalment of I Am … , Dominic Savage’s anthology series that examines different aspects of women’s lives and tends to do so with merciless precision and in pitiless detail. The stories are worked out with the female actor central to each: Vicky McClure in 2019’s inaugural I Am Nicola, about coercive control, Samantha Morton in one about the vulnerabilities poverty brings, Suranne Jones imploding under the accumulated pressures of midlife and trying to be everything to everyone because nobody else will pick up the slack, and other heavy hitters like Lesley Manville and Kate Winslet starring with younger actors to showcase different generational concerns. The latest was devised with Nicola Coughlan. Continue reading...

articles.title: Young, British and Tradwife review – TV this frustrating should come with a blood pressure warning
articles.description: Film-maker Poppy Jay meets a woman who uses her kids for money-making content and another who treats her husband like Jesus. You just wish for even more interrogation – and for a therapist to step in Like film-maker and journalist Poppy Jay’s previous (excellent) documentary, Young, British and Anti-Abortion , her latest offering should come with a warning and blood pressure medication for all women watching. Some men, too, I’m sure, but you’ll forgive me if I can’t quantify the proportion. In Young, British and Tradwife, Jay interviews three women in the UK who are advocating the lifestyle that first took off as a social media phenomenon in the US (where the evangelical Christianity and social conservatism with which it is enmeshed are stronger influences than here). Each of the trio has been chosen with care and balance to represent slightly different manifestations of the movement. Continue reading...

articles.title: The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings
articles.description: If you discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds when consuming fruit and vegetables you are missing out on a lot of value. Here’s what to incorporate into your diet – and what to avoid Do you peel your potatoes, deseed your squash and core your cauliflower? A study by King’s College London , published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition , found that people who routinely discard peels, skins, stalks and seeds when preparing fruit and vegetables are missing out on a valuable source of dietary fibre. Ten out of the 12 types of produce the researchers analysed had higher levels of fibre in the scraps than in the flesh. Eating these often overlooked parts could help address the global dietary fibre deficit and tackle food waste, they say. Here, experts share their advice on how to cook and eat “root to tip”. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘His wife was horrified’: did Edward Hopper paint his sexual problems?
articles.description: He is the maestro of American melancholy. But in a new biography, the artist is called a ‘sadist’ and a ‘prize hog’ by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.” Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. Jo once contemplated writing her husband’s biography herself, having amassed such an overwhelming body of material documenting their tumultuous marriage. As Edward’s creative partner, muse, curator, producer and unofficial manager, Jo produced 35 years’ worth of daily dia

articles.title: Don’t wait for a change in the age of consent. Adults can act to stop age-gap abuse | Gaby Hinsliff
articles.description: The law is important, but so is the fact that people know when associates embark on inappropriate relationships. They bear responsibility too Mia Latter was 16 and out clothes-shopping when Russell Brand stopped her on the street. He riffled through her bags to choose a dress he told her she should wear for the date he’d be taking her on. And so began a short relationship – if that’s the right word, given she was still at school and he was a 30-year-old MTV presenter, who she says publicly referred to her as “the child”. Towards the end, she claims, Brand orally raped her . Lilly Creightmore was 18 when she says the then 32-year-old celebrity David Walliams asked her to dinner and then began pestering her for sex. There’s a hauntingly awkward photograph of her with him at a celebrity bash. Another time, at a house party, a fellow guest remembers her sitting on the floor alone, like a bored child. She now feels his behaviour was an abuse of power over someone vulnerable. Walliams’s lawyers say he denies grooming her or behaving inappropriately. Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. So what happens next?
articles.description: The wait for the new Bond is over but that’s only the beginning – there are still small issues such as the script, title, setting, casting, branding and promotion … • Robert Pattinson announced as James Bond – news • Share your thoughts on the casting • Peter Bradshaw’s take • Pattinson’s journey to James Bond • Behind Bond’s bankability It’s official: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond . While never a certainty for the role, for those reading the runes inside the film industry, the announcement will have been a tiny bit anticlimactic. Ever since it emerged that the film’s producers appeared unsatisfied with their initial shortlist and called in Pattinson alongside Nicholas Hoult, it appeared that in this new era for Bond under Amazon MGM, the traditional Bond barrier against an established Hollywood leading man was no longer in place. And with no shade to Hoult, Pattinson’s record at delivering in major franchises – Twilight, The Batman, Dune – as well as his classy acting CV put him firmly in the driving seat. In another departure from traditional 007 practice, Amazon MGM announced the casting decision via posts on social media , rather than at a press call in a fancy London

articles.title: Milburn calls for welfare state ‘revolution’ as landmark youth unemployment report to be published – UK politics live
articles.description: Alan Milburn says his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, but overall savings will take years Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people This is what the opposition parties have been saying about the Alan Milburn proposals. The full report has not formally been published yet, but it has been circulating in Westminster on an embargoed basis since yesterday and so the parties all know what it says. The Conservatives says Milburn should be cutting welfare more aggressively. This is from Helen Whately , the shadow work and pensions secretary. Conservatives agree with Alan Milburn on the problem, and we want his review to succeed. Where Milburn gets it right, we’ll back him. Especially where he adopts our proposals like shifting from cash sickness benefits to support for milder conditions and cutting national insurance for young people. Alan Milburn is right to criticise the tax and regulation burdens Labour have imposed on businesses. But his review is too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state. Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in gove

articles.description: Zelenskyy praises ‘unprecedented attack’ but Kremlin claims bridge will be restored and will be ‘better than ever’ Europe live – follow latest Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation. articles.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
articles.description: New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients. But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market . Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 live: first draft of agreement under pressure as climate negotiations enter final days
articles.description: Thorny divisions emerge as wide-ranging draft deal seeks to ‘draw out parties’ on areas of disagreement Thousands of miles away from where negotiators are grappling over how to address the serious impacts from a warming world, the California coast is experiencing a glimpse of what’s to come. The severe effects of a historic El Niño have dramatically raised sea levels along the shores of the western US, and enormous ocean waves are chewing through swaths of the coastline. Beachside homes have been destroyed by the conditions that have also harmed marine ecosystems. Continue reading...

articles.title: Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so
articles.description: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy unpicked Darwinian sexism to rewrite the story of evolution. Now, she’s turned her attention to the nature of fatherhood ‘Spit here, dear,” Sarah Blaffer Hrdy said to her husband, Dan, handing him a vial when he arrived in New York after the birth of the couple’s first grandchild. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones. It did, although it took a day longer. In her latest book, Father Time: A Natural History of Men and Babies , Hrdy records with justified pride that “this was the first time anyone had demonstrated a bump in oxytocin levels among doting grandparents”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
articles.description: Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come. Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable. Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm Continue reading...

articles.title: Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings
articles.description: National Gallery, London Bringing together all the pioneering master’s portraits for the first time reveals the way he clinically preserved monsters, merchants – even his wife – like flies in amber The stubble is tiny yet silver-sharp on the chin of an unknown old man whom Jan van Eyck painted in oils 600 years ago: so long after both are dead you can still see this bloke needs a shave. The hairs on top of his head are just as miraculously caught, varying individually in paleness and lankness. You feast your eyes on the sagging skin of his throat with its overhangs and shady gulleys like a rock formation. He is a wonder, a freak of nature and yet a perfectly ordinary person. So are we all banal and marvellous, mundane and impossible, suggests Van Eyck. The National Gallery has created a jewel box of a show bringing together all Van Eyck’s portraits as we define them – a painting of a person for its own sake. Yet portraitist was a long way from being his only job. Van Eyck painted stupendous religious works, including the Ghent Altarpiece that he collaborated on with his brother Hubert. These too have portraits in them, of real people in uncanny proximity to supernatural beings. You

articles.title: Simply telling the AA about my minor no-fault, no-claim prang doubled my insurance quote
articles.description: A recent £364 renewal quote suddenly increased to an extortionate £796 My car was involved in a minor no-fault accident. The other driver admitted responsibility and said they would pay for repairs without involving insurers. I informed my insurer, the AA, without making a claim. It had recently sent a renewal quote for £364, but after reporting the accident I was sent a revised figure of £796.86. I was told by a call handler that any insurance company would do the same. However, they eventually lowered the quote to £452.31. This seems extortionate for a no-fault, no-claim prang. Continue reading...

articles.title: Rocky is Philadelphia’s founding myth – and 50 years later, we’re still telling it
articles.description: As Sylvester Stallone’s Oscar-winning drama celebrates its 50th anniversary, I Play Rocky helps to further turn the boxing hero into the stuff of legend The story behind the making of Rocky has always sounded uncannily like Rocky itself. An unknown with an improbable dream, a skeptical establishment and a refusal to accept the odds: Sylvester Stallone’s real-life struggle to crack the industry and bring his breakthrough film to the screen contained all the elements of the underdog story he sought to tell. Now, half a century later, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky has crafted those parallels into a crowd-pleasing yarn of its own. It’s an extraordinary afterlife for a modest boxing flick that became the highest-grossing film of 1976 on a $1m budget and won the Oscar for best picture over one of the most stacked fields in history. Yet its greatest achievement may be the durability of the story – dismissed then by the New York Times as a “sentimental little slum movie” and Gene Siskel as a “flatout schmaltzy saga” – that we’re still finding new ways to repurpose all these years later through six Rocky films, three Creed sequels, a Broadway musical , and too many documentaries, novelizati

articles.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
articles.description: It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing? In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate . In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble. Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m . Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers

articles.title: Automated warfare is already here. Now governments must restrain it | Helen Clark
articles.description: AI systems can allow militaries to find and annihilate targets within seconds. A meaningful treaty must prioritise human control – and accountability Helen Clark is former head of the UN Development Programme and former prime minister of New Zealand, and member of The Elders Militaries around the world are increasingly relying on artificial intelligence to find, track and annihilate targets. An upcoming conference in Geneva offers a chance to confront the gravest risks of AI-enabled warfare, ideally through a treaty to regulate autonomous weapons systems. A strike that might have taken half an hour and required significant human consideration only a few years ago can now take minutes, or even seconds, with AI systems taking the lead if they meet a confidence threshold set by a human operator. Helen Clark is former head of the UN Development Programme and former prime minister of New Zealand, and member of The Elders Continue reading...

articles.title: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis
articles.description: The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele. The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me ). But after working with the food magazine Vittles on its inaugural London vegan guide , I have begun to challenge the “death of vegan dining” narrative that I had found myself perpetuating. And yes, a depressing number of my choices for the Vegan 99 closed while I was writing it; mo

articles.title: I built a reputation as a ‘walker’ so I could cheat when it mattered most – and it worked | The Secret Cricket Coach
articles.description: Cricket always celebrates sportsmanship and condemns cheating, but where exactly is the line between the two? I once played in a one-day semi-final. We were in a very tight spot when I edged the ball to the keeper. I didn’t walk. The opposition couldn’t believe it. They crowded around me, furious, and I was getting plenty of abuse. I managed to get a single and when I reached the other end the umpire said: “You didn’t nick that did you? You are a walker.” “Yep, that’s right,” I replied. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Breakdown | Rattled All Blacks face rare twin threat as England eye back-to-back scalps
articles.description: After their seismic defeat by Wales, New Zealand face the prospect of history repeating itself in unwanted ways They still talk about the last – and only – time the All Blacks have contrived to lose twice in succession to England. Back in 2002-03, as now, there was a Rugby World Cup looming in Australia and New Zealand had no shortage of quality players. “There is so much talent in New Zealand that, if they don’t win the World Cup, there should be an inquiry,” opined Steve Hansen, Wales’s head coach at the time, ahead of England’s fateful visit to Wellington in the summer of 2003. There’s a fresh inquiry under way now even before the All Blacks trot out of the Twickenham tunnel this weekend for the 48th meeting between the two nations. While Saturday’s 35-28 defeat to Wales ended a 73-year wait from a home perspective it has inevitably precipitated plenty of dark muttering back in the land of the long flat white. Continue reading...

articles.title: Blackburn Rovers head coach Tony Mowbray steps down due to health issues

Mowbray was diagnosed with bowel cancer in 2024 and had to stand down from his role at Birmingham but was given the all-clear and after a spell at West Brom last year, he joined Blackburn for a second spell in June. articles.title: Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling
articles.description: Midfielder’s under-21s winner eclipsed Jude Bellingham’s mark and there was other talent to admire against France There may have been an Mbappé on the pitch – Ethan, the younger brother of Kylian, with whom he shares a near-identical gait – but by the end there was only one precocious talent on the lips of those watching England overcome France in their under-21s clash. Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling. Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal’s under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. This time last year, after taking to the field at Slavia Prague aged 15 and 308 days, Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the Champions League. In March, six months on from his professional debut, he became the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer. He is the youngest player to earn a Premier League winner’s medal. Last month he wa

articles.title: ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award
articles.description: By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria in 2022. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.” Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to BigShoe’s initiative. Continue reading...

articles.title: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta
articles.description: Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February , but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”. Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head. articles.title: Fifa accused of climate ‘record of failure’ due to Aramco deal and tournament expansion
articles.description: Groups question ‘sincerity’ to meet emissions pledges Oil giant is a major sponsor of football governing body The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action. Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”. Continue reading...
